title: The Pentagon Called India a 'Critical Anchor.' Then India's Defence Secretary Held 12 Meetings in 48 Hours.
excerpt: At the Shangri-La Dialogue, the US committed to Javelin co-production with India and demanded 3.5% GDP defence spending from allies. India responded with its most aggressive diplomatic blitz in years.
body:
The Pentagon has called India a "critical anchor" for regional stability, as US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth delivered an unusually direct endorsement of New Delhi's strategic role at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore over the weekend. In the same forty-eight hours, India's Defence Secretary held more than a dozen bilateral meetings — with the US Indo-Pacific Command, NATO's military chief, a US Congressional delegation, Singapore's president, and senior officials from Sweden, the Netherlands, and Canada.

Taken together, the engagements mark the most concentrated burst of Indian defence diplomacy in years, coming at a moment when oil prices have topped $96 a barrel, the Middle East conflict is escalating, and the Indo-Pacific order feels less stable than at any point since the pandemic.

## 'A Powerful India Advances Our Shared Goal'

Speaking on the second day of the Shangri-La Dialogue, Hegseth left little ambiguity about Washington's view of India's place in the new security architecture. "In South Asia, India is a critical anchor to hold the line," he said. "A powerful India acting in its own self-interest advances our shared goal of maintaining a balance of power across the region."

He praised India's military modernisation, particularly its expanding role in the Indian Ocean, and highlighted a concrete step that has been years in the making: co-production of Javelin anti-tank guided munitions, a weapon system long restricted to the closest of US allies. "Real, tangible steps to improve the collective readiness of our forces," he said.

Hegseth also outlined a historically large US defence spending plan — President Trump's proposed $1.5 trillion defence budget for the current fiscal year — and demanded that allies and partners commit at least 3.5 percent of GDP to defence. "For those nations that rise to this challenge, the benefits will be clear," he said, signalling that countries willing to invest would be "moved to the front of the line" for cooperation.

## India's Diplomatic Blitz on the Sidelines

While Hegseth's speech set the frame, India's Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh turned the sidelines of the Dialogue into a series of substantive meetings. He held talks with Admiral Samuel Paparo, Commander of the US Indo-Pacific Command, on strengthening military-to-military cooperation and addressing emerging security challenges in the region.

In a notable engagement, Singh met Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, Chair of the NATO Military Committee — an interaction that underscored India's willingness to engage with the Western military alliance even as it maintains strategic autonomy. The Ministry of Defence said the exchange focused on "evolving global security challenges" and "strategic dialogue."

Singh also met a US Congressional delegation, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, Sweden's State Secretary for Defence Peter Sandwall, and the Netherlands' Chief of Defence General Onno Eichelsheim. Each meeting carried a specific agenda, from defence technology partnerships to military exchange programmes.

## The India-Canada Thaw Continues

Separately, in New Delhi, Canada's High Commissioner Christopher Cooter met Defence Secretary Singh to discuss next steps in defence cooperation. The meeting followed Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's February 2026 visit to India, which produced five MOUs and commitments to expand collaboration in defence, critical minerals, and AI. The diplomatic relationship — badly frayed over the Nijjar affair — is being stitched back together, one institutional meeting at a time.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly five million Indians in the United States and Canada, the accelerating defence partnership carries practical implications. Co-production agreements create industrial jobs in both countries, potentially opening new professional avenues for the skilled Indian diaspora, particularly engineers, scientists, and tech professionals working in defence-adjacent industries in North America. This fosters cross-border collaboration and talent exchange, strengthening professional ties between the two nations. The $1.5 trillion US defence budget will flow partly through Indian defence contractors and their American partners, creating economic opportunities that resonate across the diaspora's professional networks. Furthermore, the tightening of Indo-Pacific security architecture directly shapes the geopolitical environment in which the diaspora lives and works. A more stable and secure Indo-Pacific, bolstered by these partnerships, can also indirectly benefit NRIs by ensuring smoother trade routes, predictable economic conditions, and potentially easing concerns about regional conflicts that could impact family and investments back home in India.

The Javelin co-production announcement, in particular, moves India into a category occupied by very few countries — those trusted enough to jointly manufacture frontline American weapon systems. Whether this leads to broader technology sharing or remains a carefully bounded initiative will depend on the execution in the months ahead.

**Sources:** The Indian EYE, Ministry of Defence (India), Reuters
